title: How to search the RizzitGO spreadsheet when the first page misses your find
summary: Work from a category, a short query and a recognizable detail to a shortlist you can compare and reopen.

sections.heading: Choose the clue that can actually narrow the list
paragraphs: A black pair of trousers with side pockets can appear under dozens of names. Searching for the entire caption from a social post asks the seller to have used exactly the same vocabulary as the person who posted it. Start with the part of the description you trust most. If you know the garment is a pair of trousers, enter Pants & shorts. If the picture is all you have, open image search with the camera beside the search box. If someone sent you the original listing, save that address before doing either.

The homepage contains a selection of recent items. Open Browse finds to reach the spreadsheet. Its range counter shows where the visible cards sit within the current results. After choosing a category or searching for a word, read that counter again. A smaller total tells you that a filter took effect. If you expected thousands of products and see a short list, look at the active category and the contents of the search field before starting over.

sections.heading: Try one change per search
paragraphs: Imagine you want a light rain jacket with a hood and a zip pocket at the chest. Begin with the jacket category and the word “rain.” Look at the first few relevant titles. A seller may call a lightweight shell a windbreaker. Try “windbreaker” as a separate search, leaving the category unchanged. If the title gives you a model code that is visible on the original garment, write it down exactly. A short model code can be a better second query than a long string of general characteristics.

Terms such as “black,” “hood” and “lined” can be useful once you know how the seller described the item. A title may cover ten colors and mention none of them. If your strongest candidate disappears when you add a color, return to the broader results and inspect its style selector. That decision separates a weak name match from a genuinely missing option. Keep the search narrow enough to browse but broad enough to include listings that describe a whole family of garments.

sections.heading: Read the three sorting choices
paragraphs: Latest brings recent catalog entries forward. That is helpful if you have been browsing regularly and want to see what has appeared since last time. Popular gives you a different way into a crowded category. Treat it as a browsing order. A popular card still needs the same checks for dimensions, available styles and price as a newly listed one. Price sorting is especially useful when several cards already describe the same kind of item and you want to compare the lower-priced candidates first.

Before comparing two displayed amounts, set a single currency in the header. Open each candidate and check which item the displayed price refers to. A listing whose cover shows a matching outfit may sell the jacket, trousers and set as separate options. Compare jacket with jacket and set with set. Record any difference between the displayed catalog price and the amount shown for the selected option at the purchasing platform. The latter is what matters when you decide whether to continue.

sections.heading: Find your place again on a phone
paragraphs: On a long result list, read the page number alongside the total number of pages. Use the jump field if you already know which part of the list you want. A page number has meaning only within the same search, category, sort order and page size. A friend browsing on a different device might see a different group on page three. Send the detail address of a find you want them to inspect. You can also copy its Weidian listing from the detail page when that link is available.

For a shortlist, save three things together: the individual product address, the seller's item number shown on its detail page, and a short note explaining why you saved it. “Zip pocket on the left chest, charcoal option” will mean more tomorrow than “second black jacket.” If the seller later changes a cover photo, the number gives you an independent way to check the listing. If two cards share a photograph but have different seller item numbers, keep them as separate candidates until you have compared their options.

sections.heading: Compare the detail that would change your decision
paragraphs: Set the candidates side by side and choose a single distinguishing feature. For the rain jacket, inspect where the hood drawcord exits, the shape of the sleeve cuff or whether the chest opening actually has a zip. Move through the gallery and check the selected style photo separately. Decide which observation came from a photograph and which came from the seller's written description. A photo can show a hood. It seldom settles a claim about how much rain the fabric will resist.

If neither candidate answers your question, you have a useful result from the search. You know exactly what evidence to seek. Ask for the measurement or photograph that would distinguish the two, carrying the item number and selected option into the request. Avoid sending a whole page of near-identical cards. One link and one specific question make it easier for someone else to identify the item you are discussing.

sections.heading: Finish with the correct listing
paragraphs: Open the RizzitGO purchase link from your chosen detail page. Compare the destination item number, the selected options, the quantity and the price. When a destination opens on its default color or size, select your preferred combination there. If the seller has removed that option, go back to your shortlist. A similar title alone gives you too little information to substitute a different garment. Saving the runner-up and the reason it was second lets you resume your search without having to reconstruct every filter.

title: RizzitGO Weidian links: how to share the exact color and size
summary: Learn to distinguish the catalog address, seller item number and selected SKU, then test a link before passing it on.

sections.heading: Three addresses for one pair of jeans
paragraphs: Suppose you send someone a page of jeans with forty pictured styles. They open the link, see the same cover and choose the first blue pair. You intended the dark pair with white stitching. The link reached the right listing, yet the two of you were looking at different things. A useful handover identifies both the seller's item and the combination of choices that defines the pair. This matters whenever a listing offers several washes, sizes or designs beneath one cover photo.

You may encounter three addresses along the way. The Finds Hub address takes you back to the catalog detail page and its photographs. The Weidian address points to the seller's listing. The RizzitGO button opens a buying platform's view of that listing. Each has a useful purpose. Save the catalog page for browsing, the seller link for identifying the source, and the destination details for confirming what you are about to order. A screenshot is a useful addition when two variants have very similar names.

sections.heading: Find the item number before the SKU
paragraphs: The number displayed beside Product ID belongs to the seller's item. You can use a real catalog example to see the distinction. The jeans page whose catalog path ends in 6389.html displays seller item number 7493585105. The short number in the catalog path identifies a catalog entry. The longer number appears in the source product link and the RizzitGO buying link for this example. Copy the number from the labeled field if you are sending a support request about the source product.

A SKU identifies a sellable combination within the listing. A seller might have one option group for the wash and another for the waist size. “Dark blue” selects the wash while several different waist sizes can still fit that description. If an option group lists a single value, the interface may select that value for you. Look at every group rather than counting how many times you tapped. What counts is whether the selected values identify one seller combination.

sections.heading: Select options in an order you can check
paragraphs: Start with the group containing the pictures. Enlarge the main view and compare details that distinguish the styles, such as the pocket stitching or the position of a seam. Then select the text-only fields, usually including a size if the seller provides one. Read the selected labels after each choice. A translated descriptive name may be easier to understand, while the seller number and size code are useful anchors when you change language or move to the buying platform.

Changing an earlier selection can invalidate a later one. For example, a light wash may offer sizes that a dark wash does not. After changing the wash, look at the highlighted size again. If the copy button no longer offers a style link, check whether the size needs to be selected anew. A disabled combination should prompt a new choice or a question for the seller. Guessing a combination by editing the digits in a copied link can send someone to an unrelated option.

sections.heading: Copy the style and test what survives
paragraphs: Use the style copy control once the choice is complete. Paste the result into a personal note and open it in a fresh tab before sharing it. Keep the address intact, including any part after the hash sign. Some messaging or note-taking tools shorten visible addresses, while a manually edited link may lose its variant information. Reopening the saved address is a better test than looking for a familiar product thumbnail in a message preview.

Look at the destination's displayed style and size. Different browsers, seller pages or purchasing platforms can open the correct item while leaving its choices at their defaults. If the selection is not restored, send the complete link together with the selected labels. A note such as “dark wash with white stitching, waist 32, quantity one” is easy to check against the order form. Include a cropped picture of the selected tile when the seller identifies styles only with letters, numbers or almost identical translated descriptions.

sections.heading: When the catalog offers only a product link
paragraphs: Some seller listings expose a product URL without usable option data. You may still be able to open the item and review its current choices directly at the seller. A product-level link is valuable in that situation. Record the style separately and be clear about which choices still need confirmation. A gallery photo might show an older color that is no longer selectable. Likewise, seeing a size in an image of a chart does not establish that the seller can supply that size today.

If a friend is helping with the purchase, give them a short instruction to follow when a choice has disappeared. “Please ask before substituting” works better than leaving a blank size field and assuming the intended choice is obvious. The same applies when a listing groups several pieces of an outfit. Specify whether you want the top, the trousers or the set. That wording can explain a surprisingly large price difference between two visually similar choices.

sections.heading: Check the last screen separately
paragraphs: Open the seller item through the RizzitGO purchase button or the other-agent menu. Confirm the platform domain and compare the seller item number when it is visible. Read the actual order line: its selected style, size, quantity and current amount. If your catalog link opens a general listing, reselect the combination there. Keep the order confirmation next to your note. If a later warehouse photograph shows an unexpected pair, those two records tell you whether the order itself named a different style or whether the received item needs investigation.

title: RizzitGO image search: finding a pictured item when the name is missing
summary: Choose a useful reference photo, compare the results and distinguish a bad match from a failed search.

sections.heading: Start with the part of the photograph you can recognize
paragraphs: A screenshot of a whole outfit gives a search tool several possible subjects. The jacket, shirt, shoes and wall behind them all occupy parts of the same image. If you want the bag, save a second copy and crop around the bag before uploading it. Leave the outline, the handle and a little surrounding space. Those details help you recognize the right object in a returned photo. Google gives similar advice about selecting a smaller region for a more specific visual search. On this catalog you can prepare the crop in your phone's photo editor.

A small detail can be less useful than the whole object. A close-up of a black zipper offers little evidence about the bag to which it belongs. Begin with the entire bag, then try a tighter view if several returned items have the same shape. Keep the original screenshot. It gives you another reference when comparing hardware, strap placement and scale, even if the first crop produces a better set of results.

sections.heading: Decide which kind of picture to try
paragraphs: A seller's cover is useful when you remember the listing but lost the link. Start with the original cover if you have saved it. If a seller put six colors together in one image, try the full image first. When you are searching for one particular color, also try the individual style tile if you have a clear copy. These images carry different information. A match to the collage may identify the listing while leaving the exact color unresolved.

Warehouse and detail photos answer a different question. A close shot of a heel panel could lead to a listing that shares that detail even when its cover shows the entire shoe. Use a second image from a different angle to narrow the candidates. If you have a left and a right shoe photographed separately, keep track of which side is visible. A pocket, an emblem or a panel can legitimately disappear when the opposite side faces the camera.

sections.heading: Use the camera beside the search field
paragraphs: Open the catalog's image search using the camera control or the Image search navigation link. Choose a saved image from your device. The page also offers drop and paste controls for browsers that support them. Use an ordinary still image such as JPEG or PNG. If a phone saves a picture in a format the uploader declines, export a copy in a supported format. Changing the letters at the end of the filename alone does not convert the picture.

After choosing the file, look for its preview. If it appears, check that it shows the intended crop before judging the results. An old screenshot thumbnail can look deceptively similar in the file picker. Allow the search to finish and read the status message. Choosing the same file again during an active search can restart work. On a phone, keep the tab open until results appear so you can distinguish a slow first search from a file that the browser failed to read.

sections.heading: Read similarity as a shortlist
paragraphs: Work through the first few candidates with one question in mind. What visible feature would rule out the item? If the reference has two separate front pockets, a result with one wide pocket is a poor match even when the fabric and lighting look identical. Move to the next result. For sneakers, you might compare the silhouette of the sole, the arrangement of the lace holes and the shape of the heel. A shared background or the same general color can make unrelated products look surprisingly close.

Open a promising result and inspect the gallery at full size. Check the seller's item number and any style options that correspond to your reference. The same promotional photo may be used for several listings. A visual match alone cannot establish which seller supplied the item in the screenshot. It also cannot establish material composition, current availability or the size selected by the person who took the picture. Use the image to find a candidate and the listing details to decide what you can confirm.

sections.heading: Diagnose an unsuccessful attempt
paragraphs: When no preview appears, concentrate on the input. Check that the file opens in your normal photo viewer, that it fits the size limit shown by the site and that its format appears in the upload prompt. Try saving a simple JPEG copy. A screenshot of a single item can also be a useful test. If that works while the original does not, you have narrowed the issue to the original file or how it was exported.

When a preview appears but the catalog cannot load, a tighter crop is unlikely to fix that particular attempt. Check the connection, return to the image search page and use the retry control when offered. When results load but all are visually weak, try the opposite strategy. Change the crop or choose a better angle. Add a text search in a separate tab using a distinctive feature from the photo. A short description such as “shoulder bag” can narrow your browsing while you keep the image results available for comparison.

sections.heading: Save the evidence that led to a match
paragraphs: Once you identify a likely item, bookmark its detail page and keep the crop that led you there. Add a brief note describing the matching features and any discrepancy, such as a different strap buckle. If a second person needs to choose a color or size, send the seller link and selected labels as well. That gives them a usable starting point even if their image search returns the candidates in a different order or the seller changes the listing's cover.

title: How to choose a clothing size from a RizzitGO find
summary: Compare a seller’s chart with a garment you own, resolve half-width and length conventions, and request a useful measurement.

sections.heading: Start with something you already wear
paragraphs: Choose a garment that fits in the way you want the new one to fit. If you are shopping for a jacket to wear over a sweatshirt, use a jacket that works over that same sweatshirt. A thin T-shirt from your wardrobe is a poor comparison even if both pieces have the same letter on the label. Close the jacket as you normally wear it, lay it on a level surface and smooth the fabric without pulling it tight.

Write down what you like about the reference. Perhaps the chest has enough room while the cuffs sit slightly too low. That tells you which numbers to treat as targets and which to change. You might want the new coat to have similar chest room but a shorter sleeve. Saving a photograph of your tape placement alongside the figures makes the comparison repeatable. A number without a starting point can mean something quite different when you return to it the next day.

sections.heading: Establish what the seller measured
paragraphs: Find the chart for the exact style you are considering. Look for the unit, the measurement labels and an illustration of the garment or body. A finished garment chart describes the clothing laid out or measured according to the seller's instructions. A body chart relates a person's measurements to recommended sizes. A chest value of 100 centimetres cannot be interpreted reliably until you know which kind of chart you have. A retailer such as UNIQLO publishes both conventions and distinguishes the two in its measurement guidance.

Check whether a horizontal value is a flat width or a circumference. Imagine your reference sweatshirt measures 54 cm straight across the chest. Doubling that flat measure gives an approximate 108 cm around the garment at that level. A seller may report either figure. Compare 54 with another flat width, or 108 with a comparable garment circumference. If a chart just says “chest 54” next to a picture of a person, look for clarification before converting anything. A diagram or a seller's written answer can settle the convention.

sections.heading: Match the tape positions on tops
paragraphs: For a straightforward chest comparison, lay the top flat and measure from one underarm to the other. Take the length at the location shown on the seller's diagram. A back measurement starting at the base of the collar and a front measurement starting near the shoulder can differ, particularly on a curved hem. Repeating the seller's method makes the difference you calculate meaningful. If your tape passes over a fold or along an open jacket front, straighten the garment and try again.

Sleeves take extra care. A seam at the shoulder gives you one possible starting point. A measurement from the center back of the neck to the cuff includes part of the shoulder. Comparing one method with the other can make a normally proportioned sleeve look much longer than expected. Dropped shoulders also shift where a conventional shoulder seam lies. For an unfamiliar cut, ask for a photograph identifying both ends of the sleeve measurement. Check that the answer refers to your exact style and selected size.

sections.heading: For trousers, read the rise alongside the waist
paragraphs: Measure a reference pair buttoned, zipped and laid flat. Note the waistband width at rest and the inseam from the crotch seam to the hem. If the seller gives a stretched waistband measurement, record that separately. An elastic waistband can expand by very different amounts depending on how hard someone pulls it. A comfortable resting width and the seller's stated range tell you more than a single maximum number that requires tension to reach.

Pay attention to the rise when two pairs share a waistband measurement. The rise changes where the waistband will sit on your body, so the same measured opening can feel different in use. Also inspect the thigh and hem measurements if you want a particular leg shape. A pair can match your reference at the waist and inseam while fitting much closer through the thigh. If the page includes several cuts, check the image or chart label to see which cut the figures describe.

sections.heading: Work through a comparison before selecting a size
paragraphs: Here is an illustrative example, with numbers chosen only to demonstrate the method. Your sweatshirt measures 54 cm across the chest, 67 cm in back length and 60 cm from the shoulder seam to the cuff. Candidate M measures 54, 64 and 60 by the same conventions. Candidate L measures 57, 67 and 62. M keeps your preferred width and sleeve but finishes three centimetres higher. L matches the length while adding room in the body and extending the cuff.

There is no automatic answer in those figures. Fold the hem of your own sweatshirt up by three centimetres and check where it lands over the trousers you usually wear. Turn the sleeves down by the candidate difference if the construction allows, or use another garment with a comparable sleeve. If your decision depends on a small difference, ask whether the seller states a measurement tolerance for that style. Do not borrow a tolerance from a different retailer or product chart.

sections.heading: Carry the size choice through the order
paragraphs: Once you have chosen a size, select the color and cut first if they affect which sizes appear. Recheck the size after changing any earlier option. Save the chart, the original item number and the final option labels together. If the purchasing page opens with a default selection, choose the intended combination again and compare it with your note. Recording the chart now also helps if the seller replaces its images after you place the order.

When checking warehouse pictures, ask for a measurement that resolves a specific remaining doubt. “Please photograph the back length from the base of the collar to the hem on my selected medium” gives a clear starting point, endpoint and size. Ask the platform which services are available and what they cost before requesting extra photographs. If the tape is angled, the zero mark is hidden or the garment is folded, explain which part of the measurement you need to see again before deciding whether the fit is acceptable.
